segments.text: A heart is placed on a scale. On the other side sits a single feather, the sign of Maat, truth and right order. People often say that the heart had to be lighter than the feather, and that if it failed, a monster would devour it. This is the famous Weighing of the Heart, from the Egyptian Book of the Dead. It sounds like a terrifying final exam. But what does the book itself actually say?

segments.text: First, there was no single Book of the Dead. These texts were known by phrases such as going forth by day. In the New Kingdom, selections of these spells came to be written on papyrus scrolls and buried with the dead. The choice and order of spells varied from scroll to scroll. On some, the owner's name was written in later, in spaces left blank. Some scrolls held only a few spells. Others held more than a hundred and fifty.

segments.text: The name Book of the Dead is modern. In 1842, the German scholar Karl Richard Lepsius published a long papyrus kept in Turin, under the title the Book of the Dead. His numbering of its spells became the basis of the numbers scholars still use today. The judgment we are looking for is mainly in Spell 125.

segments.text: Scholars call this the Negative Confession. Its lines are short and plain. Here are a few, from different versions, in an old English translation. I have not stolen. I have done no murder. I have spoken no lies. I have made no man to weep. I have not turned back water at its springtide.

segments.text: But what if the heart disagreed? For the Egyptians, the heart was the center of thought and feeling. It was believed to remember what a person had done. So another spell, Spell 30B, speaks directly to the heart. In an old translation, it begins, My heart my mother. It asks that nothing oppose the dead person at the judgment, and that the heart not be parted from them before the keeper of the scales. Modern translators read it as a plea that the heart not speak against its owner.
